opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's really where a lot of this work started. The naive hope, years ago, was that you could open up a model, look at a single neuron, and say "this neuron detects cats" or "this neuron fires on French text." Sometimes you do find neurons like that. But when you look at language models systematically, most neurons turn out to be what we call polysemantic. A single neuron might fire on academic citations, Korean text, HTTP requests, and something about baseball. If you try to explain the model's behavior in terms of that neuron, you don't get a clean story, because it's doing a bunch of unrelated things at once.

The reason, we think, is something called superposition. The model needs to represent far more concepts than it has neurons. There are millions of things it might want to track: specific people, places, grammatical structures, whether you're inside a code block, and so on. It only has a few thousand dimensions per layer. So it packs many concepts into the same space, using directions that aren't aligned with any single neuron. That works because most concepts are sparse. In any given context, only a small number of them are active, so the model can tolerate a bit of interference between them.

Features are our attempt to undo that compression. We train a separate model, a sparse autoencoder or more recently a transcoder or cross-layer transcoder, that takes the model's internal activations and re-expresses them in a much larger basis. We push it to be sparse, so only a handful of these units are active at a time. What falls out tends to be far more interpretable. You get a feature for the Golden Gate Bridge, a feature for "this is a rhyme I need to complete," or a feature for "the user is asking about something dangerous." They're monosemantic, or at least much closer to it, than raw neurons.

Once you have features, you can do the interesting part, which is tracing how they interact. In our circuit tracing work, we build attribution graphs. Those show, for a specific prompt, which features influenced which other features, all the way from the input tokens to the output. That lets you see, for example, that the model does multi-step reasoning internally. It might go from "Dallas" to "Texas" to "Austin" when asked for the capital of the state containing Dallas. Or it plans ahead when writing a rhyming line. You could never read that off individual neurons, because the computation is smeared across them.

I'd add one caveat. Features aren't a perfect ground truth. The replacement model doesn't capture everything, and some of the computation ends up in error terms we can't fully explain. So it's a lens. It's a much better lens than neurons, but we're still working on making it sharper.

r001.rationale: The response says most neurons are polysemantic and gives examples of one neuron responding to unrelated concepts.

r002.rationale: It explains that concepts are packed into directions that are not aligned with any single neuron, indicating representations are distributed across neurons.

r003.rationale: It describes features as much closer to monosemantic and gives examples of features for identifiable concepts.

r004.rationale: It says features are sparse and interpretable, but does not state that a feature’s high activation indicates strong representation of its concept.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the short version is that neurons just turn out not to be the right unit. If you go in and look at an individual neuron in one of these models and ask, "what does this thing respond to?", the answer is almost always a mess. It'll fire on some bit of Python code, and also on a particular style of academic citation, and also on mentions of a certain kind of animal, and there's no clean story that ties those together. People call that polysemanticity, and it's really the norm, not the exception.

The reason that happens, as best we understand it, is that the model is trying to represent way more concepts than it has neurons. It's got a residual stream of a few thousand dimensions, and it needs to track, you know, millions of distinct things about the world and about the text. So it ends up packing those concepts in as directions that aren't aligned with any single neuron. A concept gets smeared across many neurons, and each neuron participates in many concepts. That's superposition.

So if neurons aren't the right basis, you need some way to recover the basis the model is actually using. That's what features are. We train these sparse autoencoders, essentially dictionary learning, that take the activations and try to decompose them into a much larger set of directions, where only a small number are active for any given input. And when you do that and go look at what comes out, the pieces are dramatically more interpretable. You get a feature that fires on the Golden Gate Bridge, in text and in images, in multiple languages. You get a feature for code that has a bug in it, or for a character in a story who is being deceptive, or for someone flattering the user. Each one is doing one thing, more or less, and you can read it.

And that matters for the downstream questions we care about. If I want to understand how the model answers a question, I want to be able to say "this part of the computation is about the capital of Texas, and this part is about the fact that it's being asked in French." I can tell that story in terms of features. I cannot tell it in terms of neurons, because every neuron is doing eight things at once. Same thing when you want to intervene. If you can find the feature for a concept, you can turn it up or down and watch the model's behavior change in a predictable way, which is both a great test that you've found something real and, eventually, a potential tool.

I'd add one caveat, which is that features are a hypothesis about what the model is doing, not ground truth. The dictionary we learn is an approximation. It misses some of what's going on, it sometimes splits one concept into several features or merges things it shouldn't, and the right number of features is genuinely unclear. So I don't want to oversell it. But compared to staring at neurons, it's the difference between having a vocabulary for the model's internals and not having one, and that's what lets you start building up circuits and actually trace the reasoning end to end.

r001.rationale: It says individual neurons respond to a mix of unrelated things and identifies this as polysemanticity.

r002.rationale: It says a concept is smeared across many neurons and each neuron participates in many concepts.

r003.rationale: It describes features as interpretable directions, each doing one thing more or less, with examples tied to identifiable concepts.

r004.rationale: It says features fire on particular concepts, but does not state that a feature’s high activation indicates the model is strongly representing that concept.

astra-6.text:
The main reason is that individual neurons often don’t correspond to a single, coherent concept. You might find a neuron that activates for several seemingly unrelated things. So if you look at that neuron and ask, “What does it represent?” it’s hard to give a useful answer.

One way to think about this is that the model has more concepts it wants to represent than it has neurons available. It can represent those concepts using overlapping patterns of activity across neurons. That’s what we call superposition. A feature, in this picture, is a pattern of activity that we’re trying to disentangle from those overlapping representations.

For example, we might recover a feature that responds to a particular concept across different contexts, even though no individual neuron cleanly tracks it. That gives us a more useful unit for understanding the model. We can look at when the feature activates, and then intervene—turn it up or down—and see how that changes the model’s behavior.

That doesn’t mean every feature has a neat human-readable meaning, or that we’ve completely understood the model. But it gets us closer to studying meaningful concepts rather than individual coordinates in its internal representation.

r001.rationale: The response says individual neurons often activate for several seemingly unrelated things.

r002.rationale: It describes concepts as represented through overlapping patterns of activity across multiple neurons.

r003.rationale: It gives the example of recovering a feature that responds to a particular concept across different contexts.

r004.rationale: The response says to observe when a feature activates, but does not state that high activation means the model is strongly representing the corresponding concept.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic problem is that a neuron doesn’t necessarily correspond to one concept. You might find a neuron that activates for several seemingly unrelated things, and a particular concept might be represented across many neurons. So if you look at neurons individually, it can be hard to tell a coherent story about what the model is doing.

Features are an attempt to find a more useful unit of analysis: patterns of activity that correspond to something interpretable. A feature might respond to a particular kind of code, or a concept that shows up across different languages and contexts. It doesn’t have to line up with a single neuron; it can be a direction in the model’s activation space.

That gives us a better starting point for understanding the computation. We can ask when a feature activates, how it relates to other features, and whether changing its activation changes the model’s behavior. That last part matters, because seeing a correlation is different from understanding what actually drives an answer.

r001.rationale: The response says a neuron may activate for several unrelated things, but does not state that individual neurons are typically polysemantic.

r002.rationale: It states that a particular concept might be represented across many neurons.

r003.rationale: It says features correspond to something interpretable, but does not clearly state that each feature corresponds to a single identifiable concept.

r004.rationale: It discusses when a feature activates, but does not explain that high activation indicates strong representation of its concept.
